facts.claim: FSANZ, Allergen labelling for food businesses (read 19 November 2026; page last updated 30 September 2025): 'For food not required to bear a label (such as food provided at a café or takeaway), declarations must be displayed in connection with the food or provided to the purchaser upon request using the required names.'

FSANZ, Allergen labelling for food businesses: 'the Food Standards Code requires certain food and substances to be declared when they are present in a food as ingredients including food additives or processing aids.' Food allergy reactions can include 'anaphylaxis'.

Queensland Government Accessible Events Guide, Signage: 'Signage is a vital element of assisting attendees to navigate the venue and to effectively and efficiently access what they need. For this to work, signage needs to be clear, logical, accurate and accessible.'

Queensland Government Accessible Events Guide, Signage guidelines: 'Consistency and standardisation: information overload can be avoided with the consistent placement, size, colour and shape of signage.' and 'Simplicity: avoid visual clutter and limit each sign to three or four units of information, because people tend to glance rather than read.'

Queensland Government Accessible Events Guide, Signage: 'Set up items at the acceptable height (viewable at all heights for people in wheelchairs, children, tall people and tested in a crowd in advance) and ensure it has clear directions.' No measurement is stated.

insider_details.detail: Edible place cards (biscuits, macarons, chocolates, sugared almonds) are food given to guests, and a food allergy reaction can include anaphylaxis. Give the baker or caterer your guest allergy list before you order, and keep any edible card off the setting of a guest with a relevant allergy, or swap it for a non-edible card with the same look.

In Australia, for food that doesn't carry a label, allergen declarations must be displayed in connection with the food or provided on request. That obligation sits with the food business, not the couple, so ask the supplier of edible cards what allergen information comes with them. General information, not legal advice. For a wedding overseas, don't assume Australian rules apply: ask the venue or local baker how allergens are handled.

Readable beats clever. The Queensland Government accessible events guide asks that signage be clear, logical, accurate and accessible, and notes people tend to glance rather than read, so keep each card to the guest's name (plus a table number or meal marker if needed) in a size and colour that stands out from the material it sits on.

The same guide asks that items be viewable at all heights, including for people in wheelchairs, children and tall people. For place cards, that means a name that reads from the chair, not only from standing, and a test of one finished card at the table before the full set is made. The guide gives no measurement, so don't state a font size or height.

For a destination wedding, plan place cards that travel well or can be made locally. Stone, glass, shell and fresh-leaf or herb cards add weight or need to stay fresh; confirm with the venue what can be brought in and when the tables can be set. Advice, not a sourced fact.
